title: Account Management
plainLanguageExplanation: The organization has a defined process for creating, changing, reviewing, and disabling user accounts, so that only appropriate people have active accounts at any given time.
controlObjective: Ensure accounts are established, tracked, and maintained according to documented authorization, and that account activity can be reviewed.

evidenceRequested.label: Current account inventory report
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Exported within the last 30 days, includes account status and owner

evidenceRequested.label: Sample of account creation approvals
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Shows requestor, approver, and business justification

evidenceRequested.label: Documented account management procedure
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Current version, reviewed within the last 12 months

evidenceQualityCriteria: Evidence is timestamped and covers the audit period
Approvals are traceable to a named, authorized approver
Procedure documentation matches what is actually performed
commonEvidenceGaps: Account inventory is outdated or manually maintained in a spreadsheet
No documented approval for some active accounts
Procedure exists but is not followed consistently
exampleAuditTest: Select a sample of active accounts and trace each one back to an approved request.
exampleCompliantCondition: Every sampled account has a documented, approved request on file.
exampleAuditFinding: For 4 of 25 sampled accounts, no approval documentation could be located.
potentialSecurityRisk: Unauthorized or unapproved accounts may exist with access that was never formally reviewed.
potentialBusinessImpact: Increased risk of unauthorized data access and difficulty demonstrating control ownership during an audit.
suggestedRemediation: Reconstruct and document approval evidence for accounts missing it
Implement a standard intake form for all future account requests
Schedule a recurring account inventory export
sourceReference: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-2 (public reference; summary is original)
educationalDisclaimer: This record is for educational audit-readiness practice. It does not certify any organization as compliant with NIST SP 800-53.

title: User Deprovisioning (Leaver Process)
plainLanguageExplanation: When someone leaves the organization or changes roles, their access should be removed or adjusted promptly so former employees or old roles don't retain unnecessary access.
controlObjective: Ensure access is revoked or modified in a timely manner following a termination or role change.

evidenceRequested.label: HR termination report for the period
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Includes termination date and last day of work

evidenceRequested.label: System logs showing access removal timestamps
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Removal date is on or before the required deadline

evidenceRequested.label: Documented exceptions for delayed removals
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Includes business reason and approval

evidenceQualityCriteria: HR and IT termination dates reconcile
Removal timestamps are system-generated, not self-reported
Exceptions are approved, not just noted after the fact
commonEvidenceGaps: No reconciliation between HR terminations and IT deprovisioning
Access removed late with no documented exception
Shared or service accounts not covered by the leaver process
exampleAuditTest: Select a sample of terminated employees and confirm access was removed within the required timeframe.
exampleCompliantCondition: All sampled terminations show access removed within 24 hours of the termination date.
exampleAuditFinding: 3 of 20 sampled terminated users retained active VPN access for 5-9 days after termination.
potentialSecurityRisk: Former employees may retain the ability to access systems or data after leaving the organization.
potentialBusinessImpact: Potential data exfiltration, regulatory exposure, and reputational harm if a former employee's access is misused.
suggestedRemediation: Automate the HR-to-IT termination feed where possible
Set a hard SLA (e.g., same business day) for access removal
Add a monthly reconciliation between HR and identity system records
sourceReference: General concept aligned to NIST Cybersecurity Framework PR.AC category (public reference; summary is original)
educationalDisclaimer: This record is for educational audit-readiness practice. It does not certify any organization as compliant with the NIST CSF.

title: Least Privilege / Privileged Access
plainLanguageExplanation: People and service accounts should only have the elevated access they truly need to do their job, and that access should be tracked more closely than standard access.
controlObjective: Limit privileged access to the minimum necessary and ensure it is monitored and periodically justified.

evidenceRequested.label: Inventory of privileged/admin accounts
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Includes system, account owner, and business justification

evidenceRequested.label: PAM vault checkout/session report
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Shows who checked out privileged credentials and when

evidenceRequested.label: Manager sign-off on privileged access review
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Signed within the current review cycle

evidenceQualityCriteria: Every privileged account has a named human or system owner
PAM session logs are complete and cannot be edited by the account holder
Sign-off is from someone with authority over the account, not self-approved
commonEvidenceGaps: Standing (always-on) privileged access instead of just-in-time checkout
No PAM tool in place for some privileged systems
Reviews performed but not formally signed off
exampleAuditTest: Confirm that a sample of privileged accounts is enrolled in the PAM solution and reviewed within the last quarter.
exampleCompliantCondition: All sampled privileged accounts are vaulted and show a completed quarterly review.
exampleAuditFinding: 6 of 15 sampled admin accounts had standing access outside the PAM vault with no recent review.
potentialSecurityRisk: Excess standing privileged access increases the blast radius of a compromised credential.
potentialBusinessImpact: Higher likelihood and severity of a privileged-account-driven security incident.
suggestedRemediation: Onboard remaining privileged accounts into the PAM solution
Convert standing access to just-in-time checkout where feasible
Formalize a quarterly privileged access review with documented sign-off
sourceReference: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-6 (public reference; summary is original)
educationalDisclaimer: This record is for educational audit-readiness practice. It does not certify any organization as compliant with NIST SP 800-53.

title: Multifactor Authentication
plainLanguageExplanation: Users must verify their identity with more than just a password (for example, a password plus a phone app code) before accessing sensitive systems.
controlObjective: Reduce the risk of unauthorized access from stolen or guessed passwords by requiring an additional identity factor.

evidenceRequested.label: MFA enrollment report for in-scope systems
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Shows enrollment percentage and lists any exceptions

evidenceRequested.label: MFA policy or configuration screenshot
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Shows enforcement is applied, not just available/optional

evidenceRequested.label: Approved exceptions for accounts without MFA
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Includes compensating control and approval

evidenceQualityCriteria: Report reflects current state, not a point-in-time snapshot from months ago
Enforcement is technically confirmed, not just policy language
Every exception has a documented compensating control
commonEvidenceGaps: MFA is available but not enforced for all users
Legacy or service accounts excluded without documented justification
No compensating control identified for exceptions
exampleAuditTest: Sample a set of accounts with access to sensitive systems and confirm MFA is enforced at login.
exampleCompliantCondition: All sampled accounts are required to complete a second authentication factor.
exampleAuditFinding: MFA was not enforced for 2 legacy service accounts with interactive login capability.
potentialSecurityRisk: Accounts without MFA are significantly more susceptible to credential-based compromise.
potentialBusinessImpact: Increased likelihood of account takeover leading to data breach or fraud.
suggestedRemediation: Enforce MFA for all remaining in-scope accounts
Document compensating controls for any accounts that technically cannot support MFA
Add MFA enrollment status to new-hire and account-creation checklists
sourceReference: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, IA-2 (public reference; summary is original)
educationalDisclaimer: This record is for educational audit-readiness practice. It does not certify any organization as compliant with NIST SP 800-53.

title: Periodic User Access Reviews
plainLanguageExplanation: On a regular schedule, someone who understands what a user should have access to reviews that user's actual access and confirms it's still appropriate.
controlObjective: Ensure access remains appropriate over time and inappropriate access is identified and removed.

evidenceRequested.label: Access report used for the review
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Generated at or near the review date, covers all in-scope entitlements

evidenceRequested.label: Manager or owner certification of the review
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Signed or system-recorded approval from an authorized reviewer

evidenceRequested.label: Formal review sign-off / approval record
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Distinct from the raw access report; shows the review was completed and closed

evidenceRequested.label: Documentation of any flagged exceptions
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Explains why flagged access was kept or removed

evidenceRequested.label: Evidence that inappropriate access was removed
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Ticket or log showing removal date and who performed it

evidenceQualityCriteria: The review is recent (within the recommended frequency)
Certification comes from someone with real knowledge of the user's job duties
Flagged items are tracked to closure, not just noted
commonEvidenceGaps: Review is overdue (older than the required frequency)
Access report exists but no manager certification is on file
Flagged/inappropriate access identified but never actually removed
exampleAuditTest: Confirm the most recent access review was completed within the required frequency and that flagged items were remediated.
exampleCompliantCondition: The review was completed on schedule, certified by managers, and all flagged access was removed with evidence.
exampleAuditFinding: The quarterly user access review is 9 months overdue. The evidence folder contains only an old access report with no manager certification, review approval, exception documentation, or proof that inappropriate access was removed.
potentialSecurityRisk: Users may be carrying excessive or unauthorized access that has never been validated, increasing the risk of misuse.
potentialBusinessImpact: Regulatory or contractual non-compliance (e.g., PCI DSS), and potential unauthorized exposure of sensitive data such as cardholder data.
suggestedRemediation: Complete a full access review immediately and document manager certification
Establish exception documentation for any access that will be kept
Remove or downgrade access identified as inappropriate and log the remediation
Set a recurring calendar reminder or workflow to prevent future overdue reviews
suggestedRemediationOwner: System/Application Owner, with IAM Team support
sourceReference: General concept aligned to PCI DSS access-restriction requirements (public reference; summary is original)
educationalDisclaimer: This record is for educational audit-readiness practice. It does not certify any organization as compliant with PCI DSS.

title: Logging and Monitoring of Privileged Activity
topic: Logging and monitoring of privileged activity
plainLanguageExplanation: Actions taken by privileged/admin accounts should be logged and someone should actually be watching those logs for suspicious activity.
controlObjective: Detect misuse or compromise of privileged accounts through timely logging, alerting, and review.
recommendedReviewFrequency: Continuous monitoring; monthly log review sign-off

evidenceRequested.label: SIEM/log source coverage report for privileged systems
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Confirms in-scope systems are actively sending logs

evidenceRequested.label: Documented alert rules for privileged activity
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Rules map to specific risky privileged actions

evidenceRequested.label: Monthly log review sign-off
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Shows a named analyst reviewed and closed the period

evidenceQualityCriteria: Log coverage is verified technically, not assumed
Alerts are tuned to reduce noise while still catching real risk
Review sign-off happens on schedule, not retroactively bulk-signed
commonEvidenceGaps: Privileged systems exist outside SIEM/log collection scope
Alerts configured but no one is assigned to triage them
Log review sign-off is missing or done in bulk long after the period
exampleAuditTest: Confirm a sample of privileged systems are sending logs to the SIEM and that alerts triggered in the period were reviewed.
exampleCompliantCondition: All sampled privileged systems are logged and monitored, with documented review of triggered alerts.
exampleAuditFinding: 2 of 8 privileged systems were not forwarding logs to the SIEM during the review period.
potentialSecurityRisk: Malicious or accidental privileged activity could go undetected.
potentialBusinessImpact: Delayed detection and response to a security incident involving privileged access.
suggestedRemediation: Onboard the missing privileged systems to the SIEM
Assign clear ownership for triaging privileged-activity alerts
Institute a monthly sign-off process for log review completion
sourceReference: General concept aligned to CIS Controls v8, Control 8 (public reference; summary is original)
educationalDisclaimer: This record is for educational audit-readiness practice. It does not certify any organization as compliant with CIS Controls.

title: Segregation of Duties
plainLanguageExplanation: No single person should have conflicting access that lets them both create and approve the same transaction (for example, creating a vendor and also approving payments to that vendor), because that combination creates an opportunity for fraud or error to go undetected.
controlObjective: Prevent any one individual from having enough access to complete an entire high-risk process end to end without independent oversight.
recommendedReviewFrequency: Quarterly, plus at every role or access change

evidenceRequested.label: Segregation of duties conflict matrix
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Lists defined conflicting access combinations for the in-scope application

evidenceRequested.label: SoD violation/exception report
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Generated from actual current access, not a manual list

evidenceRequested.label: Documented mitigating controls for accepted conflicts
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Explains the compensating control and who approved keeping the conflict

evidenceQualityCriteria: The conflict matrix reflects the actual business process, not a generic template
The violation report is system-generated against current entitlements
Every accepted conflict has a named compensating control and approver
commonEvidenceGaps: No formal SoD matrix exists for the application
Violations are known informally but never formally reported or tracked
Mitigating controls are assumed but not documented or tested
exampleAuditTest: Run the SoD ruleset against current access and confirm every flagged conflict has an approved, documented mitigating control.
exampleCompliantCondition: All flagged conflicts have a documented, approved compensating control on file.
exampleAuditFinding: One user retained both 'create vendor' and 'approve payment' access in the ERP system with no documented mitigating control.
potentialSecurityRisk: A single compromised or malicious account could complete a fraudulent transaction end to end without independent review.
potentialBusinessImpact: Financial statement misstatement risk and potential SOX control deficiency finding.
suggestedRemediation: Remove or restrict one side of the conflicting access where feasible
Document a compensating control (e.g., independent transaction review) where access cannot be separated
Formalize a recurring SoD conflict report as part of the access review cycle
sourceReference: General concept aligned to SOX logical-access control expectations (public reference; summary is original)
educationalDisclaimer: This record is for educational audit-readiness practice. It does not certify any organization as compliant with the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.

title: Service Accounts
plainLanguageExplanation: Non-human accounts used by applications, scripts, and integrations should have a named human owner, a documented purpose, and credentials that are managed and rotated just like any other privileged access — not left running forever with a password no one remembers setting.
controlObjective: Ensure service accounts are inventoried, owned, and managed to prevent them from becoming an untracked, unmonitored path to sensitive systems.
controlOwner: IAM Team Lead, with System Owner co-ownership

evidenceRequested.label: Service account inventory
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Includes named human owner, purpose, and system(s) accessed for every entry

evidenceRequested.label: Credential rotation history
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Shows rotation occurred within the defined policy interval

evidenceRequested.label: Evidence the account is vaulted or centrally managed
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Credential is not stored in plaintext scripts or shared documents

evidenceQualityCriteria: Every service account has exactly one named accountable human owner
Rotation evidence is system-generated, not a manual claim
No credentials are found hard-coded or stored outside an approved vault
commonEvidenceGaps: Service accounts exist with no documented owner ("orphaned" accounts)
Passwords have never been rotated since creation
Credentials are stored in scripts, spreadsheets, or shared drives instead of a vault
exampleAuditTest: Select a sample of service accounts and confirm each has a named owner, a documented purpose, and evidence of credential rotation within policy.
exampleCompliantCondition: All sampled service accounts have a current owner, documented purpose, and rotation evidence within the required interval.
exampleAuditFinding: 5 of 12 sampled service accounts had no assigned owner, and 3 had not been rotated in over two years.
potentialSecurityRisk: Orphaned or unrotated service account credentials are a common path for long-term, low-visibility compromise.
potentialBusinessImpact: Undetected lateral movement or persistent access in the event of a breach, and difficulty responding quickly during an incident because no owner can be identified.
suggestedRemediation: Complete a full service account discovery and assign an owner to every account
Migrate credentials into an approved vault/PAM solution
Establish and enforce a rotation policy with automated reminders
Decommission accounts with no identifiable business purpose
sourceReference: General concept aligned to CIS Controls v8, Control 5 (public reference; summary is original)
educationalDisclaimer: This record is for educational audit-readiness practice. It does not certify any organization as compliant with CIS Controls.

title: Joiner-Mover-Leaver (JML) Lifecycle
plainLanguageExplanation: As people join the organization, change roles, or leave, their access should be granted, adjusted, or removed to match — with special attention to role changes, since old access often quietly lingers after a transfer or promotion.
controlObjective: Ensure access stays aligned with a person's current role throughout their employment lifecycle, not just at hire and termination.

evidenceRequested.label: HR role/transfer change report for the period
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Includes effective date of the role change and prior/new role

evidenceRequested.label: Evidence access was adjusted following the role change
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Shows both new access granted and old access removed, with dates

evidenceRequested.label: Documented exception for any retained legacy access
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Includes business justification and approval

evidenceQualityCriteria: Role change dates from HR reconcile with access adjustment dates in IT
Both the grant and the removal side of a transfer are evidenced, not just one
Retained legacy access has a documented, approved reason
commonEvidenceGaps: New access is granted for the new role but old role access is never removed
No formal trigger connects HR role changes to an access review
Transfers between departments are not tracked as consistently as terminations
exampleAuditTest: Select a sample of employees who changed roles in the period and confirm old-role access was removed within the required timeframe.
exampleCompliantCondition: All sampled role changes show old access removed and new access granted within the defined SLA.
exampleAuditFinding: 7 of 15 sampled employees who transferred departments retained one or more access rights from their prior role more than 60 days after the transfer.
potentialSecurityRisk: Accumulated legacy access from past roles ('access creep') increases the risk of excessive or inappropriate access going unnoticed.
potentialBusinessImpact: Violation of least-privilege expectations and potential exposure of data outside an employee's current job function.
suggestedRemediation: Establish a formal trigger from HR role-change events to an access adjustment workflow
Require manager attestation for both the new and prior role's access during a transfer
Add role-change reconciliation to the quarterly access review process
suggestedRemediationOwner: IAM Team Lead, with HR partnership
sourceReference: General concept aligned to NIST Cybersecurity Framework PR.AC category (public reference; summary is original)
educationalDisclaimer: This record is for educational audit-readiness practice. It does not certify any organization as compliant with the NIST CSF.

title: Password and Authentication Management
plainLanguageExplanation: Passwords and other authenticators (like tokens or certificates) should meet defined strength and management requirements, and there should be a documented process for how they're issued, changed, and revoked.
controlObjective: Ensure authenticators are strong enough and managed well enough to resist compromise throughout their lifecycle.

evidenceRequested.label: Password policy configuration export
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Reflects current enforced settings (length, complexity, expiration), not just written policy

evidenceRequested.label: Sample of authenticator issuance/reset records
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Shows identity verification occurred before issuance or reset

evidenceRequested.label: Attestation that no shared or default credentials remain in use
evidenceRequested.qualityCriteria: Covers default vendor passwords and shared logins specifically

evidenceQualityCriteria: Policy export is a live system configuration screenshot or export, not just a written policy document
Identity verification steps for resets are evidenced, not assumed
Default and shared credentials are explicitly tested for, not just assumed absent
commonEvidenceGaps: Written policy exists but technical enforcement doesn't match it
Help desk resets don't consistently verify caller identity
Default vendor passwords remain unchanged on some systems
exampleAuditTest: Compare the documented password policy to the actual enforced configuration, and test a sample of systems for default or shared credentials.
exampleCompliantCondition: Enforced configuration matches documented policy, and no default or shared credentials are found in the sample.
exampleAuditFinding: 2 of 10 sampled systems were still using vendor-default administrator passwords.
potentialSecurityRisk: Weak, default, or shared credentials are one of the most common initial access points in real-world breaches.
potentialBusinessImpact: Increased likelihood of unauthorized access and difficulty attributing actions to a specific individual when credentials are shared.
suggestedRemediation: Change all identified default vendor credentials immediately
Align technical policy enforcement with the documented password standard
Add identity verification steps to the help desk reset procedure
sourceReference: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, IA-5 (public reference; summary is original)
educationalDisclaimer: This record is for educational audit-readiness practice. It does not certify any organization as compliant with NIST SP 800-53.
